raw_case_text:
A 13-month-old boy, the second child of consanguineous parents, was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) of the Children's Hospital of Chongqing Medical University in October 2018. He presented with a paroxysmal cough for 1 month, aggravated with shortness of breath and wheezing for 1 week. Regarding the patient's family history, there was nothing unusual in the immune system. The child was delivered naturally at full term and has received his BCG vaccination. There was no history of feeding difficulties or repeated respiratory tract infections. He had not been exposed to toxic substances, gases, smog, or allergens.
A chest CT scan at a local hospital revealed a bilateral lung infection. The treatment of cefminox and interferon-alpha1b was not effective. The cyanosis was difficult to relieve. The patient was then admitted to our hospital with endotracheal intubation for further treatment. At admission, the boy had malnutrition with a normal body temperature and oxygen saturation of 94% under assisted ventilation (other vital signs were as follows: heart rate of 147 beats/min, the respiration rate of 30 beats/min, bodyweight of 5.5 kg, blood pressure of 77/50 mmHg). Nasal flaring, cyanosis around the lips, and an inspiratory triple concave sign were observed. Chest auscultation revealed bilateral coarse crackles.
Chest radiographs showed decreased translucency in both lungs and an extensively increased density shadow in the alveoli, showing ground-glass changes. Some showed a mesh change, a slightly dilated bronchus, and localized hyperinflation of the upper lobe of the left lung. Lung injury caused by a diffuse interstitial lesion of both lungs and ARDS were considered (Figure 1). The blood routine on admission showed that the white blood cell counts were elevated (18.91 x 109/L) (reference value: 4.3-11.3 x 109/L), neutrophils mainly, and a thrombocyte count of 490 x 109/L (reference value: 100-453 x 109/L), a hemoglobin concentration of 121 g/L (reference value: 118-156 x 109 g/L), and a slightly elevated level of C-reactive protein (CRP) (9 mg/L) (reference value: <8 mg/L); other markers were within the reference ranges. After treatment with piperacillin-tazobactam for 4 days and meropenem for 6 days, the inflammatory indicators gradually decreased. However, on the 10th day of hospitalization, the white cell count and the neutrophil percentage increased again, and the level of CRP increased to 20 mg/L. The platelet count increased with the continuous decrease of red blood cells and hemoglobin (81-121 g/L), and the child had no bleeding tendencies. Amphotericin B, meropenem, and cefoperazone-sulbactam were administered as treatment, but the patient's condition did not improve. The level of CRP had no obvious change (18-20 mg/L), the white blood cell count continued to rise (12.25-18.45 x 109/L), and the level of hemoglobin decreased to 77 g/L. Arterial blood gas analysis indicated type 2 respiratory failure (PO253 mmHg, PCO262 mmHg). After admission, the assisted ventilation was continued, and the patient still had persistent oxygenation disorders. The child had hypoproteinemia, increased lactate dehydrogenase, and a decrease in cholinesterase. Immunoglobulin levels (including IgM, IgG, and IgA) were in the normal range. The C3 complement was 0.43 g/L. Tumor markers were negative. Flow cytometry was used for the detection of T cell, B cell, NK cell and other lymphocyte subsets were determined, with no obvious abnormalities (CD4/CD8 2.37, CD3 + 1610.88/mul, CD3 + CD8 + 457.59/mul, CD3 + CD4 + 1084.62/mul, NK cell 53/mul). The TREC gene was detected by fluorescence probe PCR screening for severe combined immunodeficiency diseases. The result was >1,000 copies/mul (<10 copies/mul is considered to be severe combined immune deficiency, 10-1,000 copies/mul is considered to be a primary immune syndrome or normal, and >1,000 copies/mul is considered normal). The fungal D-glucan test, T-SPOT test, purified protein derivative test, Mycoplasma pneumonia/Chlamydia PCR, sputum bacterial and fungal culture, and double blood were negative. Pneumocystis was not detected in the next-generation sequencing (NGS) of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid, and CT findings did not support pneumocystis Jiroveci pneumonia. All tests were negative for influenza virus A and B, respiratory syncytial, adenovirus, parainfluenza 1, 2, and 3, coronaviruses (including HKU-1, OC43, 229E, NL63), rhino/enterovirus, parechovirus, Hanta pulmonary syndrome, and fungi. The results of metagenomics NGS (mNGS) in serum and respiratory secretions suggested that HBoV had a high detection sequence of 112,786 reads and 100% gene coverage. The coverage of Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas fluorescens, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa were 0.889%, 0.058%, and 0.005%, respectively, and the reads were 370, 14, and 2, which were considered colonized bacteria. The mNGS was carried out by a core facility (Kindstar Global, Wuhan, China). HBoV was the only viral pathogen detected. No other pathogens were detected. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) showed that the viral load of NPA was 2.08 x 1010 copies/ml and the viral load of serum was 2.37 x 105 copies/ml. Viral DNA and RNA were extracted from 200-microl aliquots of the NPA samples by the QIAamp MinElute Virus Spin kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). The RNA was applied as the template for complementary DNA (cDNA) synthesis with the SuperScript III First-Strand Synthesis System (Invitrogen, California, USA). DNA and RNA extractions and cDNA products were used for the subsequent testing of respiratory viruses. HBoV1-specific primers were forward primer amplification of 5'-CCTATATAAGCTGCTGCACTTCCTG-3' and reverse primer 5'-AAGCCATAGTAGACTCACCACAAG-3'. The plasmid amplified target fragment was cloned into the pMD19-T vector (TaKaRa Biotechonology, Dalian, China). The PCR process was performed exactly as described in the report, except for the AmpErase-UNG at 50 C. Each run included plasmid and negative controls. Standard precautions were taken throughout the PCR process to avoid cross-contamination. Negative controls and serial dilutions of the positive controls were included in every PCR assay. Therefore, HBoV was considered to be the pathogen in this case. Finally, the boy was diagnosed with severe pneumonia, ARDS, and diffuse pulmonary interstitial disease.
Due to the high suspicion of the possibility of respiratory system-related genetic diseases, complete exon sequencing (completed by Beijing Mygeno) was completed during hospitalization. It indicated that the patient had a heterozygous variant in the STAT1 gene: C. 1127 + 10G > A, causing amino acid change splicing. After 16 days of treatment in the ICU, the patient's pulmonary symptoms were not alleviated, and the chest CT scan showed that the diffuse lesions in both lungs were still severe. The patient's family was required to give up treatment, and the patient died.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 13-month-old boy born to consanguineous parents presented in October 2018 with a 1-month history of paroxysmal cough aggravated for 1 week by shortness of breath, wheezing, and refractory cyanosis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child developed a paroxysmal cough 1 month prior to admission, which worsened 1 week before referral with acute shortness of breath, wheezing, and cyanosis. At a local hospital, a chest CT showed bilateral lung infection, and treatment with cefminox and interferon-alpha1b failed to relieve his refractory cyanosis, requiring endotracheal intubation and transfer to our pediatric ICU.
subjective.past_medical_history: Full-term vaginal delivery; BCG-vaccinated; no prior history of feeding difficulties, recurrent respiratory infections, or toxic/allergen exposures. Family history: Second child of consanguineous parents, with no known family history of immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for paroxysmal cough (1 month), shortness of breath, wheezing, and perioral cyanosis (1 week).

objective.physical_examination: Admission vital signs and anthropometrics (intubated on assisted ventilation): Severe malnutrition with body weight 5.5 kg, normal body temperature, heart rate 147 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min, blood pressure 77/50 mmHg, and SpO2 94%. Physical findings: Nasal flaring, perioral cyanosis, inspiratory three-depression (suprasternal, intercostal, subcostal) retractions, and bilateral coarse crackles on chest auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission hematology and biochemistry: Leukocytosis with WBC 18.91 x 10^9/L (reference: 4.3–11.3 x 10^9/L, predominantly neutrophils), thrombocytosis with platelets 490 x 10^9/L (100–453 x 10^9/L), hemoglobin 121 g/L (dropping to 77 g/L by day 10), and C-reactive protein (CRP) 9 mg/L (<8 mg/L, rising to 20 mg/L on day 10); hypoproteinemia, elevated LDH, decreased cholinesterase, and low complement C3 (0.43 g/L). Arterial blood gas (day 10): Type 2 hypercapnic and hypoxemic respiratory failure with PO2 53 mmHg and PCO2 62 mmHg. Immunological and microbiological screening: Normal serum IgG, IgA, and IgM; negative tumor markers, T-SPOT.TB, PPD, Mycoplasma/Chlamydia PCR, sputum bacterial/fungal cultures, two sets of blood cultures, and standard respiratory virus panel. Chest radiographs: Decreased bilateral lung translucency with diffuse ground-glass and reticular/mesh alveolar opacities, mild bronchial dilatation, and localized left upper lobe hyperinflation.
objective.advanced_workup: Lymphocyte subsets, TREC assay, and fungal biomarker: Normal flow cytometry subsets (CD4/CD8 ratio 2.37, CD3+ 1,610.88/μL, CD3+CD4+ 1,084.62/μL, CD3+CD8+ 457.59/μL, NK cells 53/μL); normal TREC count >1,000 copies/μL; negative serum fungal beta-D-glucan test. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and serum metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) and quantitative PCR (qPCR): BAL mNGS and chest CT were negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii; respiratory secretion and serum mNGS identified human bocavirus 1 (HBoV1) with 112,786 sequence reads and 100% genome coverage (plus minor colonization reads of Acinetobacter baumannii [370], Pseudomonas fluorescens [14], and P. aeruginosa [2]); HBoV1-specific qPCR confirmed an extremely high viral load of 2.08 x 10^10 copies/mL in nasopharyngeal aspirate and 2.37 x 10^5 copies/mL in serum. Whole-exome sequencing (WES): Identified a heterozygous splice-site variant in the STAT1 gene (c.1127+10G>A).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Fatal severe human bocavirus 1 (HBoV1) viremia and interstitial pneumonia complicated by pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and type 2 respiratory failure in a malnourished 13-month-old boy carrying a heterozygous STAT1 splice-site variant (c.1127+10G>A), definitively confirmed by mNGS (112,786 HBoV reads, 100% coverage) and qPCR (NPA 2.08 x 10^10 copies/mL, serum 2.37 x 10^5 copies/mL) with Pneumocystis jirovecii excluded by BAL mNGS and beta-D-glucan testing. Plan and clinical course: Managed in the PICU with invasive mechanical ventilation and sequential piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, cefoperazone-sulbactam, and amphotericin B; after 16 days of refractory respiratory failure and unimproved diffuse bilateral lung lesions on CT, the family withdrew life support and the child died.
